key: D major in the orchestral original; band version transposed
intro: The United States Marine Band plays Elgar’s first Pomp and Circumstance march, with its long singing tune surrounded by quick, sharp-edged music. Woodwind and brass carry both sides of its character.

cues.title: With much fire
cues.text: Elgar heads the march Allegro, con molto fuoco: fast, with much fire. Its opening phrases strike off the beat, then hurry on in short bursts. The United States Marine Band carries that orchestral music into woodwind and brass.
cues.evidence: Elgar’s orchestral score, opening Allegro con molto fuoco: https://imslp.org/wiki/Pomp_and_Circumstance_March_No.1,_Op.39_No.1_(Elgar,_Edward). The Marine Band performance is identified by its Commons source; the arranger is unidentified.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Room for the long tune
cues.text: The trio brings the melody later sung as Land of Hope and Glory. Its phrases climb, rest on long notes and answer with falling steps. Beneath it, the accompaniment keeps a steady two-beat tread.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal I, Trio: melody and accompaniment. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/6e/IMSLP24159-PMLP23738-Elgar_-_Pomp_and_Circumstance%2C_Op._39%2C_No._1.pdf. The cue describes the tune at the established trio boundary in this band arrangement.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Elgar in Yale blue
cues.text: At Yale on 28 June 1905, Elgar receives an honorary doctorate and puts on the university’s blue robes. The orchestra plays this march as the guests leave. Other universities adopt it, and the tune becomes part of American graduation ceremonies.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society, Why Americans graduate to Elgar: the degree ceremony, blue robes, recessional and later adoption. https://www.elgar.org/3pomp-b.htm

cues.title: The quick phrases return
cues.text: The march comes back with its short, accented phrases and runs of quick notes. The long melody pauses for a whole section while the bass and tune resume their brisk exchange.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal M: return of the quick march. This arrangement’s established returning-march boundary is 3:20; the note concerns the shared themes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Benson supplies the words
cues.text: In 1902, A. C. Benson gives the trio melody words for Elgar’s Coronation Ode, then revises them for the separate song Land of Hope and Glory. Clara Butt sings the solo version. The tune now carries an appeal for an expanding British Empire.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society describes Benson’s versions, Clara Butt’s performance and reproduces the texts, including the appeal for wider imperial boundaries. https://www.elgar.org/3pomp.htm

cues.title: The march has the last word
cues.text: The broad tune finishes, but the march has a few quick phrases left. Short notes dart through the closing passage before a sharp accent and the final held chord.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal T to the end: a tempo and Più mosso. The band recording’s established coda boundary is 5:30; no particular instrumental allocation is asserted.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.note: Rule 1, recording-specific US-law basis under 17 USC §105, not worldwide CC clearance. Commons separates Performance/Recording from Composition and attributes the file to a Marine Band official-duty recording with an official .mil source. No CC-NC licence appears in the Commons record or the reviewed official source wording. Marine Band boilerplate says its institutionally distributed recordings ‘may not be distributed for private use and are not for sale’ because appropriated funds are used: this is the agency’s physical-distribution policy, not a non-commercial copyright licence on the government performance. Official web downloads are offered separately. Direct upstream retrieval returned HTTP 403 during this research; the official page’s indexed distribution wording and reader-accessible download instructions were examined, and the file’s recording-specific Commons declaration remains explicit. No claim of worldwide rights or a cleared private arrangement is made.

composer.epithet: He made the Enigma Variations from his friendships and preserved his own way with the music on gramophone records.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. His education continued in rehearsal rooms. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn from inside the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. Here was an orchestra whose players he knew individually, with capabilities he had to accommodate. His other work included teaching in local schools and giving private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
